newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns of Internet job, business scams.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns of Internet job, business scams.

text.p: Scam artists have seized on the Internet to promote fraudulent business opportunities, preying on college graduates and out-of-work professionals, the Federal Trade Commission said on Tuesday.

"Thanks to personal computers, desktop publishing software and affordable video equipment, bogus sales pitches have the look of legitimacy and lure millions of consumers to take the bait," said an FTC report, "Fighting Consumer Fraud: The Challenge and the Campaign."

Business schemes are a big part of consumer fraud the FTC said costs Americans a reported $250 million a year -- and far more fraud likely goes unreported. Shady promoters aim at recent college graduates or out-of-work professionals, frequently promising job placement with Fortune 500 companies, the federal government or travel carriers such as cruise ships and airlines, the report said.
Con artists retain processing or finder's fees they charge, it said. Or they use personal financial information to debit client bank accounts or use credit cards.

Working with the FBI and postal inspectors, the FTC has brought seven actions against nine companies and 16 people who promised, falsely, to obtain jobs for consumers. "By the end of 1996 these efforts had produced more than $1 million in refunds for tens of thousands of consumers," said the agency, which has reponsibility for consumer protection.

The FTC warned those seeking jobs to be suspicious of any promises to find them a job, especially if the company charges fees in advance or guarantees refunds. Job seekers should be aware some services place ads that seem to offer jobs when in fact all they have to sell is job information.
It also advised job seekers to check with the corporate offices of any company listed in an advertisement to find out if the company is really hiring.
And watch out for firms promoting supposedly "undisclosed" federal government jobs. "All federal positions are announced to the public," the FTC said.
The federal government and 25 state attorneys general have also completed 75 law enforcement actions against scam artists offering business opportunities.

People looking for business opportunities should ask for a disclosure document on any franchise or business opportunity, the government said. These documents are required by law and would-be investors should beware of any company without them.
Investors should also obtain a complete list of current franchise or business opportunity owners. Warns the FTC: "A list of references selected by the company is no substitute."
The FTC also suggested investigating any earnings claims. For example, demand to see the company's basis for its claims in writing.
